response.title: Can I plug my travel trailer's power cord straight into a power station to run the lights, fan and microwave for a weekend with no hookups?
response.answer:
Yes! You can plug your travel trailer's shore-power cord directly into a portable power station and run the lights, fans, microwave, and other appliances for a weekend without hookups.

The key is choosing a power station with enough output power (watts) to run your appliances and enough battery capacity (watt-hours) to last the weekend.

1. How to connect it
Shop
Shop
Shop
Shop
Shop
Shop
Shop

Typical 30A RV shore-power plug and portable power station setup.

Most travel trailers use a 30-amp, 120V shore-power connection.

You can connect it using:

Power station with a 30A RV outlet (TT-30): Plug your trailer cord directly into it.

Power station with standard 120V outlets: Use a properly rated 15A-to-30A RV adapter.

A standard 120V outlet is typically limited to 15A or 20A, regardless of the trailer's 30A plug. Turn off high-draw appliances you aren't using, especially the air conditioner, electric water heater, and electric space heater.

2. How much power will you need?

Here is an example of electricity usage over a two-night, approximately 48-hour camping weekend.

Appliance

	

Estimated usage

	

Weekend energy




LED lights

	

30W × 5 hr/day

	

300 Wh




Roof vent fan

	

25W × 10 hr/day

	

500 Wh




Microwave

	

1,500W × 10 min/day

	

500 Wh




Water pump

	

60W × 15 min/day

	

30 Wh




Miscellaneous electronics

	

20W × 10 hr/day

	

400 Wh




Total

		

1,730 Wh

Allowing for inverter losses and some reserve, I'd plan for approximately 2,300–3,000 Wh of battery capacity for this example.

Your trailer's converter may also draw power to charge its house battery, increasing consumption. A refrigerator, furnace blower, or other loads could change the estimate substantially.

3. What size power station should you get?
Shop

2,000 Wh class

Good for basic lighting, fans, device charging, and occasional microwave use. May need recharging during a weekend.

Shop

4,000 Wh class

More comfortable for a two-night trip, with additional reserve for appliances and unexpected loads.

For the microwave, look for at least 2,000W continuous AC output, preferably more. A microwave advertised as 1,000W cooking power can consume 1,500W or more electrically.

4. Important things to check

Grounding and neutral: Some power stations have floating-neutral outputs that may not work properly with certain RV electrical protection systems. Check compatibility with your trailer's electrical system and any EMS/surge protector.

Trailer battery: If your trailer has a house battery, its 12V lights, fans, and water pump may already work without shore power.

Converter: When plugged into a power station, the RV converter may charge the house battery, wasting energy through repeated conversions. Consider the converter's role in your setup before switching it off.

Air conditioning: Running the rooftop AC is a much bigger load and requires a different battery-sizing calculation.

markup:
**Yes! You can plug your travel trailer's shore-power cord directly into a portable power station** and run the lights, fans, microwave, and other appliances for a weekend without hookups.

The key is choosing a power station with enough **output power (watts)** to run your appliances and enough **battery capacity (watt-hours)** to last the weekend.

## 1. How to connect it

<box gap={2}>
  <AsyncImageGroup query={["travel trailer 30 amp RV shore power cord TT-30 plug","portable power station connected to RV 30 amp shore power cord camping"]} aspectRatio="5:3" shop_eligible={true}/>
  <text color="secondary" size="xs">Typical 30A RV shore-power plug and portable power station setup.</text>
</box>

Most travel trailers use a 30-amp, 120V shore-power connection.

You can connect it using:

- **Power station with a 30A RV outlet (TT-30):** Plug your trailer cord directly into it.
- **Power station with standard 120V outlets:** Use a properly rated 15A-to-30A RV adapter.

A standard 120V outlet is typically limited to 15A or 20A, regardless of the trailer's 30A plug. Turn off high-draw appliances you aren't using, especially the air conditioner, electric water heater, and electric space heater.

## 2. How much power will you need?

Here is an example of electricity usage over a two-night, approximately 48-hour camping weekend.

| Appliance | Estimated usage | Weekend energy |
|---|---|---:|
| LED lights | 30W × 5 hr/day | 300 Wh |
| Roof vent fan | 25W × 10 hr/day | 500 Wh |
| Microwave | 1,500W × 10 min/day | 500 Wh |
| Water pump | 60W × 15 min/day | 30 Wh |
| Miscellaneous electronics | 20W × 10 hr/day | 400 Wh |
| **Total** | | **1,730 Wh** |

Allowing for inverter losses and some reserve, I'd plan for approximately **2,300–3,000 Wh of battery capacity** for this example.

Your trailer's converter may also draw power to charge its house battery, increasing consumption. A refrigerator, furnace blower, or other loads could change the estimate substantially.

## 3. What size power station should you get?

<box gap={3}>
  <row align="start" gap={3}>
    <AsyncImage query="EcoFlow DELTA 2 Max portable power station product white background" aspectRatio="1:1" maxWidth="124px" shop_eligible={true}/>
    <box flex="1" gap={1}>
      **2,000 Wh class**

      Good for basic lighting, fans, device charging, and occasional microwave use. May need recharging during a weekend.
    </box>
  </row>
  <divider color="subtle"/>
  <row align="start" gap={3}>
    <AsyncImage query="EcoFlow DELTA Pro 3 portable power station product" aspectRatio="1:1" maxWidth="124px" shop_eligible={true}/>
    <box flex="1" gap={1}>
      **4,000 Wh class**

      More comfortable for a two-night trip, with additional reserve for appliances and unexpected loads.
    </box>
  </row>
</box>

For the microwave, look for at least **2,000W continuous AC output**, preferably more. A microwave advertised as 1,000W cooking power can consume 1,500W or more electrically.

## 4. Important things to check

- **Grounding and neutral:** Some power stations have floating-neutral outputs that may not work properly with certain RV electrical protection systems. Check compatibility with your trailer's electrical system and any EMS/surge protector.
- **Trailer battery:** If your trailer has a house battery, its 12V lights, fans, and water pump may already work without shore power.
- **Converter:** When plugged into a power station, the RV converter may charge the house battery, wasting energy through repeated conversions. Consider the converter's role in your setup before switching it off.
- **Air conditioning:** Running the rooftop AC is a much bigger load and requires a different battery-sizing calculation.

## 5. Let me size it for your trailer

{@body const [amps,setAmps] = DIL.useState("30")}
{@body const [battery,setBattery] = DIL.useState("yes")}
{@body const [loads,setLoads] = DIL.useState(["lights","fan","microwave"])}
{@body const [nights,setNights] = DIL.useState("2")}
<box border radius="xl" padding={3} gap={3}>
  <form gap={3} onSubmit={()=>GenUI.issueNewTurn("Size a portable power station for my travel trailer. Shore power: "+amps+" amps. House battery: "+battery+". Appliances: "+loads.join(", ")+". Trip length: "+nights+" nights. Recommend battery Wh, inverter W, and hookup considerations.")}>
    <box gap={1}>
      <label>Trailer shore-power connection</label>
      <radio-group direction="row" value={amps} onChange={setAmps}>
        <radio value="30">30 amp</radio>
        <radio value="50">50 amp</radio>
        <radio value="unknown">Not sure</radio>
      </radio-group>
    </box>
    <box gap={1}>
      <label>Does your trailer have a house battery?</label>
      <radio-group direction="row" value={battery} onChange={setBattery}>
        <radio value="yes">Yes</radio>
        <radio value="no">No</radio>
        <radio value="unknown">Not sure</radio>
      </radio-group>
    </box>
    <box gap={2}>
      <label>What do you want to run?</label>
      <grid columns={2} gap={2}>
        {#each [{id:"lights",name:"LED lights"},{id:"fan",name:"Roof vent fan"},{id:"microwave",name:"Microwave"},{id:"fridge",name:"Refrigerator"},{id:"furnace",name:"Furnace blower"},{id:"ac",name:"Air conditioner"},{id:"tv",name:"TV / electronics"},{id:"pump",name:"Water pump"}] as item}
          <grid-item key={item.id}>
            <checkbox checked={loads.includes(item.id)} onChange={v=>setLoads(p=>v?[...p,item.id]:p.filter(x=>x!==item.id))} lineThrough={false}>{item.name}</checkbox>
          </grid-item>
        {/each}
      </grid>
    </box>
    <box gap={1}>
      <label>How long will you camp without hookups?</label>
      <radio-group direction="row" value={nights} onChange={setNights}>
        <radio value="1">1 night</radio>
        <radio value="2">2 nights</radio>
        <radio value="3">3 nights</radio>
        <radio value="4+">4+ nights</radio>
      </radio-group>
    </box>
    <button block submit>Calculate my power station needs <icon name="arrow-right" inline/></button>
  </form>
</box>

With those details, I can estimate whether a 2 kWh station is enough or whether a 4 kWh unit makes more sense, without overspending on capacity you won't use.
